text: Raw data rarely has exactly the columns your analysis needs. You compute totals, flag categories, bucket numbers into bands, and fix types. In SQL that's the select list with expressions and case when. In pandas, you create new columns by assignment. This lesson covers the six moves you'll use constantly. We continue with the illustrative orders table, working on a copy to keep the original safe.

Assign to a column name that doesn't exist yet, and pandas creates it — the math is vectorized, so it applies to every row at once. Multiply amount by 1.08 and round to 2 places to get amount underscore with underscore tax — order 1's 120.50 becomes 130.14. Notice the missing amount on order 5 simply stays missing, NaN, after the math — missing values propagate through arithmetic instead of raising an error.

SQL's case when maps to np dot where, taking a condition, a value if true, and a value if false. Label every order size as large when the amount is 100 or more, small otherwise — one line, applied to every row at once.

For three or more categories, use np dot select, which takes a list of conditions and a list of results, checked in order — put the strictest first. Amount 200 or more is big, 100 or more is medium, otherwise small. But here's the trap: order 5 has a missing amount, and NaN compared to 100 is False, so order 5 silently gets labeled small — a wrong answer that doesn't announce itself. When missing values matter, handle them explicitly with another condition on amount dot isna, labeled something like unknown.

Map translates each value using a dictionary, handy for grouping codes into cleaner categories. Map status values shipped to done, returned and cancelled both to issue, and pending to open. Any value not in the dictionary becomes NaN, so double-check your mapping actually covers everything in the column.

pd dot cut sorts numbers into bands — you give it the edges and a label for each band. Cut amount into bins at 0, 75, 150, and 1000, labeled low, mid, and high. Amounts from 0 to 75 are low, above 75 up to 150 are mid, and above 150 up to 1000 are high. Intervals are closed on the right by default, so an amount of exactly 75 falls into low. The missing amount, as always, stays NaN.

Astype converts a column's data type — turn order underscore id from a number into text with dot-astype of str. Rename swaps column names — rename amount to total. And drop removes columns you don't need, like customer underscore id. Rename and drop both return a new DataFrame — they don't change the original unless you assign the result back to a variable.

Apply runs a function on each value, one at a time — apply a lambda that doubles amount, for example. It works, but it's slower than vectorized math and harder to read. If you can write the same thing as arithmetic, np dot where, or map, do that instead, and save apply for logic that truly has no vectorized form.

Assign returns a new DataFrame with the extra column added, which lets you chain steps without touching the original — orders dot assign, adding amount underscore k as amount divided by 1000. One warning worth knowing: if you filter first and then add a column to the result directly, pandas may print a SettingWithCopyWarning. Fix it by calling dot-copy right after you filter, before you start assigning new columns.

To recap: create columns by assigning arithmetic, use np dot where or np dot select for conditions, map and pd dot cut for recoding and banding, and astype, rename, and drop for housekeeping. Prefer vectorized operations over apply, and remember that missing values can slip through conditions silently. Next: sorting, ranking, and counting values.
